production_notes: No facts to verify: Elif and her interviews are hypothetical (content.md Review Flags: None).
Elif is a fictional founder in Izmir, Türkiye. Shops are labelled Shop A to Shop E on screen, with no names.
Claude appears only as a slide mock-up of the pattern list, not a live screen recording (L03 is not a screen-demo lesson). Show the cleaned notes with no real personal data.

Hook.voiceover: Ask a friend, would you use an app that does this, and they will almost always say yes. It feels good, but it tells you almost nothing. Today you will learn to ask questions that people cannot answer just to be polite.

Explain.voiceover: In the last lesson, you chose a problem. Now you test it by talking to people. This is called customer discovery: talking to potential customers to learn about their problem before you build. The goal is not to sell your idea. The goal is to learn the truth.

slide.title: Customer Discovery Interviews
slide.body: Building an AI Startup · Lesson 3 of 15

Explain.voiceover: The most important rule is this. Ask about past behaviour, not opinions about your idea. Opinions about the future, like would you pay for this, are cheap and often wrong. Facts about the past, like what did you do last time, are much more reliable.

slide.title: Past facts beat future opinions
slide.body: Left (red): 'Would you pay for this?' 'Would you use an AI tool?' Right (green): 'When did this last happen?' 'What did you do?'

Explain.voiceover: Good questions sound like this. When did this problem last happen? What did you do about it? What did it cost you, in time, money or lost customers? What have you tried already? And who else is involved?

slide.title: Good questions
slide.body: When did this last happen? · What did you do? · What did it cost you? · What have you tried? · Who else is involved?

Explain.voiceover: Use a short script of about twenty minutes. Thank the person and say you are not selling anything. Ask for consent to take notes, and promise not to use their name. Do not record audio unless they agree. Ask about their normal week. Then spend most of the time on the last time the problem happened, what it cost, and what they use today.

slide.title: A 20-minute interview
slide.body: Timeline bar: Thank and explain (1 min) · Consent (1) · Context (3) · The last time (6, largest block) · Cost (3) · Current solutions (4) · Close (2)

Explain.voiceover: Close by asking who else you should talk to. And throughout, listen more than you talk. When you hear something important, just say, can you tell me more?
Explain.stock_query: person listening and taking notes interview

Explain.voiceover: Here is a picture to remember. A detective does not ask a suspect, would you ever commit a crime? She asks, where were you on Tuesday at eight in the evening? Specific questions about real events are much harder to answer with a comfortable story.
Explain.stock_query: detective writing in notebook desk lamp

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's watch this work. Elif is a made up founder in Izmir, Türkiye. She believes small shop owners lose money by running out of popular products and ordering too much of slow ones. She interviews five owners, and she does not mention AI.
Demonstrate.stock_query: small grocery shop owner behind counter

Demonstrate.voiceover: She asks a grocer, when did you last run out of something? Last Friday, bread flour, before a holiday weekend. What did you do? I sent my nephew to a wholesaler, and we lost half a day. How do you decide what to order? I look at the shelves and write a list in a notebook.

slide.title: Interview with Shop A
slide.body: Chat-style exchange. Elif: 'When did you last run out of something?' Grocer: 'Last Friday. Bread flour, before a holiday.' Elif: 'What did you do?' Grocer: 'Sent my nephew to a wholesaler. Lost half a day.' Elif: 'How do you decide what to order?' Grocer: 'I look at the shelves and write a list.'

Demonstrate.voiceover: After five interviews, Elif removes all names and labels her notes Shop A to Shop E. Then she asks Claude to list common patterns, and how many shops support each one. Claude suggests three.

slide.title: Clean first, then ask Claude
slide.body: Notes with names crossed out → labels Shop A–E → Claude prompt: 'List patterns and how many shops support each'.

Demonstrate.voiceover: One, ordering is done from memory or a notebook, in four of five shops. Two, stock problems cluster before holidays, in three of five. Three, owners want an app to predict demand. Claude says three of five.

slide.title: Claude's three patterns
slide.body: 1. Ordering from memory or a notebook (4 of 5) · 2. Stock problems before holidays (3 of 5) · 3. Owners want an app to predict demand (Claude: 3 of 5)

Demonstrate.voiceover: Elif checks her notes. Patterns one and two are correct. Pattern three is not supported. No owner asked for an app. One owner only said it would be nice to know earlier. Claude turned a wish into a request. So Elif deletes it and plans more interviews about holiday ordering.

slide.title: Check every pattern
slide.body: 1. Confirmed (green tick) · 2. Confirmed (green tick) · 3. Not supported (red cross): only 'It would be nice to know earlier.'

Demonstrate.voiceover: The most common mistake is pitching during the interview. The person politely agrees, and you leave feeling validated, but you learned nothing. Keep your idea out of the conversation, at least until the very end. A second mistake is accepting an AI summary without checking it. Every pattern should point back to real words in your notes.

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, ask about specific past events, actions and costs, not opinions about your idea. Second, use a short script, ask for consent, and listen more than you talk. Third, remove names before using AI to find patterns, and check every pattern against your own notes.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Past events and costs, not opinions. 2. Short script, consent, listen. 3. Remove names; check every AI pattern against notes.

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn. In the exercise below this video, interview three to five potential customers. Remove names from your notes, use Claude to find patterns, and check each one yourself. Plan about ninety minutes, including the interviews. Next, we look at testing demand before you build. See you there.
